newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds edge lower ahead of election day.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds edge lower ahead of election day.

text.p: Stock and bond prices edged lower Friday as investors chose to mark time ahead of Tuesday's presidential and congressional elections.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 7.45 points to 6,021.93. For the week, it was up 14.91 points.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,229 to 1,147 on heavy volume of 463 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"A lot of traders have stepped to the sidelines to see what the elections will bring," said Thom Brown, a managing director of Rutherford Brown & Catherwood.
"There's the fear of the Democrats carrying both houses of Congress and there might be a nervous reaction fearing a return of an inflationary scenario," he said.

The bellwether 30-year Treasury bond fell 14/32, or $4.375 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.68 percent from 6.64 percent at Thursday's close.

The yield briefly slipped to a 7-month low of 6.59 percent early Friday on news that the unemployment rate was unchanged at 5.2 percent in October, and job growth was at a moderate 210,000, which was in line with Wall Street expectations.
Two reports by private groups added to a picture of moderating economic activity.

A survey of the nation's purchasing managers showed that the manufacturing sector grew more slowly in October than in September. And a key forecasting gauge rose for the eighth straight month, though it was the smallest gain in that string of increases.
The reports come just two days after the government said the economy slowed to a 2.2 percent rate of growth in the third quarter from a 4.7 percent rate in the second quarter.

"Virtually all the economic data we've seen this week suggests that at the Nov. 13 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, talk will begin on an easing," said Tom Carpenter, chief economist at ASB Capital Management Inc.

The Federal Reserve's policy-setting FOMC meets later this month to weigh its next move on interest rates. Most analysts expect the central bank's policy-makers to hold rates steady and perhaps cut them sometime early next year.
In currency markets, the dollar fell against most leading currencies after former Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen said a stronger dollar could harm U.S. exporters.
In an interview with Reuters Financial Television, Bentsen said he was "comfortable" with the dollar's current strong exchange rate.
But he warned that any further gains by the dollar vs. the Japanese yen could reduce U.S. exports to Japan.
"If (the dollar) continues to rise and goes substantially above this, of course, it puts us at a competitive disadvantage. I would prefer not to see it increase in value," he said.
The dollar ended at 113.35 Japanese yen on Friday, down from 114.03 yen late Thursday and fell to 1.5143 German marks from 1.5180 marks.
In commodities trading, crude oil prices fell for the fifth straight day as worries about historically low heating oil supplies faded.
December crude oil fell 32 cents a barrel to $23.03 at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE index fell 30.6 points to 3,948.5 while Tokyo's Nikkei 225 rose 166.20 points to 20,633.06.
